dossier.public_summary: The light curve shows a very spotted star with two claimed transits thousands of ppm deep and one below noise, so the depth changes by a factor of ~20 between sectors and even between the four events and there is a strong secondary dip at the same orbital phase. Difference imaging is inconclusive but with no stable flat-bottomed transit and a deep secondary, a blended stellar eclipse (or systematic artefact on this active star) is a better explanation than a 2.5 Earth-radius planet. An odd-even difference of diff_sigma 2.95 supports the idea the true period may be 28.8 days.

reasons.why: Depth changes enormously between sectors (168% change, 1554 ppm, 995 ppm vs 81 ppm +/-115) with chi2 46.85 dof 2. Alone this is not a reject, but with other evidence it shows the signal is not a planet of steady depth.

Even when keeping the same pipeline (QLP 995 ppm, SPOC 2-min 1554 ppm, TESS-SPOC 81 ppm) each pipeline shows a single sector, so the variation is truly between observations, not just calibration. A planet should have one depth.

Individual transits are wildly inconsistent: epoch 0 1761 ppm vs epoch 48 81 ppm (sigma -6.3) with share_of_top_3 0.999. Four transits near a gap (gaps.p_chance 0.019) with top two carrying all signal point to a few bad events, not a repeating planet.

Secondary dip is strong and at the same shape phase offset as the primary, with SNR above the best brightening. Hot giant can show tiny secondary but 278 ppm vs 1010 ppm is deep; combined with variable depth and inconsistent transits this favours a stellar eclipse over a planet.

Target is a very spotted K dwarf with huge phase-curve (amplitude_ppm 102.7) whose variability can mimic or bias transits. The depth scatter and secondary are best explained by activity/BEB effects, not a 2.538 Rearth planet.
